cards.title: The AST Taxonomy: Five Ways to Test Security
cards.teaser: Application Security Testing is not one thing — it is five distinct approaches, each aimed at a different attack surface, at a different point in the SDLC. Knowing the taxonomy tells you which tool to reach for and when.

runs.text: The five categories of Application Security Testing (AST) are often conflated because vendors sell tools that span multiple categories. Treating them as distinct disciplines clarifies what each one can and cannot find.

items.text: Analyzes source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing the application. Runs early in the SDLC, often on every commit. Finds coding flaws: injection points, hardcoded secrets, unsafe API usage.

Tests a running application from the outside, like an attacker would. Requires a deployed environment. Finds runtime vulnerabilities: authentication bypass, injection, misconfigured headers, exposed endpoints.
Inventories third-party libraries and frameworks, then checks them against known CVE databases. Does not test your code — tests the code you imported.

Instruments the running application from the inside while automated tests or traffic exercises it. Combines static analysis precision with dynamic coverage — seeing exactly which code paths handle which data.
An agent embedded in production that detects and blocks attacks in real time. Not a testing tool — a runtime defense layer. Often confused with IAST because both instrument the running process.

runs.text: Each technique has a home in the SDLC. SAST runs at code review time. SCA runs at build time. IAST runs during automated testing. DAST runs against a staging environment. RASP runs in production. No single tool covers all five: a mature program uses them in layers.

Gartner coined the AST taxonomy in the early 2010s. The IAST category was added later by Contrast Security, whose founders were frustrated that neither SAST nor DAST found the class of vulnerabilities they were seeing in production.

SAST reads your code without running it. DAST pokes your running app from the outside. SCA checks your imported libraries for known bugs. IAST watches your code run from the inside. RASP blocks attacks in production. Each one sees a different slice of the risk surface.

cards.title: AST Tool Comparison: When Each Runs and What Each Finds
cards.teaser: Choosing an AST tool without understanding when it runs and what it is capable of finding leads to gaps in coverage and false confidence. This comparison maps each technique to its position in the SDLC and its characteristic finding types.

runs.text: The table below compares the four primary AST techniques across the dimensions that matter for SDLC integration:

rows: Insecure code patterns, hardcoded secrets, injection sinks, unsafe API calls
Logic flaws, auth issues, runtime misconfigs
Auth bypass, injection (HTTP), exposed headers, misconfigured TLS, open redirects
Known CVEs in dependencies, outdated packages, license violations
Actual tainted data flows, injection, deserialization, insecure crypto in executed paths
Active exploit attempts, SQL injection, command injection, path traversal at runtime

runs.text: The key insight from this comparison: SAST and DAST are
complementary, not redundant.

SAST finds what the code says it might do; DAST finds what the running system actually does. The same vulnerability can appear in both or in only one, depending on whether the code path is executed and whether the runtime environment matches the static model.

Organizations that run only SAST and skip DAST frequently miss authentication and session management flaws — the code may look correct statically but the runtime integration between components creates the vulnerability. DAST finds these; SAST does not.

SAST finds code that looks dangerous. DAST finds behavior that is dangerous. SCA finds libraries that are known to be dangerous. IAST finds dangerous data flows that actually happened during tests. They are not competitors — they cover different blind spots.

cards.title: SAST: Analyzing Code Without Running It
cards.teaser: Static Application Security Testing treats source code as structured text and asks: are there patterns here that a skilled attacker could exploit? It is the earliest signal in the pipeline — and the noisiest.

runs.text: SAST tools operate on source code, compiled bytecode, or intermediate representations (IR). The core technique is
taint analysis

: tracking data from untrusted sources (user input, HTTP headers, file reads) through the codebase to dangerous sinks (SQL queries, shell commands, HTML output). If a path from source to sink lacks sanitization, it is a finding.
Three analysis techniques underpin most SAST tools:

items.text: The simplest form. The tool parses the code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and searches for known-dangerous patterns: calls to
assignments. Fast, low-overhead, high false positive rate.

Tracks how values propagate through variables, function calls, and control flow branches. Can determine whether user input reaches a dangerous sink even across function boundaries and modules. More accurate than pattern matching; more compute-intensive.

Understands the meaning of code constructs — not just that a value is passed to a function, but what that function does with it. CodeQL represents the extreme end of this approach, modeling the entire codebase as a relational database and allowing SQL-like queries over code semantics.

runs.text: SAST integrates early in the SDLC — in IDE plugins, pre-commit hooks, and PR pipelines. This "shift-left" placement means findings reach developers while context is fresh. The tradeoff is noise: a SAST tool run on a typical codebase produces findings that include a significant proportion of false positives, and teams that do not triage systematically learn to ignore all alerts.

A SAST tool that produces 200 findings per PR, most of them false positives, is worse than no tool — it trains engineers to click "dismiss all" and ships nothing to production. Tune SAST rules aggressively before deploying in CI gates.

SAST reads your code the way a security-aware developer would — looking for places where untrusted data could reach dangerous operations. It is fast, runs without executing anything, and catches bugs early. The downside is it often cries wolf.

cards.title: CodeQL: Code as a Queryable Database
cards.teaser: CodeQL is GitHub's semantic SAST engine — it compiles source code into a relational snapshot and lets you write SQL-like queries over it. This makes it possible to find vulnerabilities that span dozens of files and function calls, not just single-line patterns.

runs.text: CodeQL was developed by Semmle (acquired by GitHub in 2019). Its central insight: instead of scanning source text,
extract a database from the code

that captures types, call graphs, data flows, and control flows, then query that database using QL (a Datalog-inspired query language). The result is that CodeQL queries are composable, version-controlled, and shareable — any team can write a query that encodes institutional security knowledge.
How CodeQL works in practice:

items.text: During the build, a CodeQL extractor captures compiler-level information — the same data the compiler uses — and stores it in a
database. This means CodeQL sees resolved types, not just text.

QL queries run against the database. The built-in query suites (Security Extended, Security and Quality) cover OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25, and language-specific patterns. Custom queries can express organization-specific rules.

Results appear as Code Scanning alerts on pull requests, with links to the exact line and a description of the vulnerable data flow. Free for public repositories; requires GitHub Advanced Security for private repos.

runs.text: A minimal CodeQL query for detecting SQL injection in Java:

explanation.code:
/**
 * @name SQL injection
 * @kind path-problem
 * @id java/sql-injection
 */
import java
import semmle.code.java.dataflow.TaintTracking
import semmle.code.java.security.QueryInjection

from QueryInjectionSink sink, RemoteFlowSource source
where TaintTracking::localTaint(source, sink)
select sink, source, sink,
  "SQL query built from $@.", source, "user-controlled input"

runs.text: This query finds all paths from
RemoteFlowSource
(HTTP request parameters, headers, cookies) to
QueryInjectionSink
(JDBC query execution points) without sanitization. The path-problem kind produces a full call-graph trace from source to sink in the results.

CodeQL's query packs (published at github.com/github/codeql) are open source. The Security Extended suite contains over 60 queries per language. Writing custom queries is the primary way organizations encode internal security policies as code.

CodeQL compiles your code into a database, then lets you run queries that ask "does user input ever reach a SQL query without being sanitized?" — across your entire codebase, following function calls wherever they lead. It is SAST done with full type and data-flow awareness.

cards.title: Semgrep: Lightweight Pattern-Based SAST
cards.teaser: Semgrep is a fast, open-source static analysis engine built for developer workflows — it matches code patterns using rules that look like the code they are finding, making custom rule authoring accessible to developers who are not security specialists.

runs.text: Semgrep was created at r2c (now Semgrep Inc.) and open-sourced in 2020. Its design philosophy is explicit: security rules should be readable and writable by the developers who maintain the code, not only by dedicated security engineers.
Semgrep rules use a pattern syntax that mirrors the language being analyzed. A rule to flag Python
subprocess.call
with shell=True:

explanation.code:
rules:
  - id: subprocess-shell-true
    patterns:
      - pattern: subprocess.call(..., shell=True, ...)
    message: >
      subprocess.call with shell=True is dangerous when arguments
      include user-controlled input. Use shell=False and pass arguments
      as a list instead.
    languages: [python]
    severity: ERROR
    metadata:
      cwe: CWE-78
      owasp: A03:2021 Injection

runs.text: Key Semgrep capabilities that distinguish it from grep-based scanning:

items.text: Semgrep parses code into an AST before matching, so
matches regardless of whitespace, line breaks, or comments between the tokens.
as wildcards that capture any expression. A rule with
matches any call to eval with any argument, and can then constrain what $X may be.

Semgrep maintains a public registry at semgrep.dev/r with thousands of community-contributed rules covering OWASP Top 10, framework-specific vulnerabilities (Django, Spring, Rails), and supply chain risks. Onboarding takes minutes.

Semgrep is written in OCaml and designed for sub-second rule evaluation. A typical repository scans in seconds, not minutes — making it practical as a pre-commit hook or in PR pipelines where developer wait time matters.

runs.text: Semgrep's primary limitation is the same as all pattern-based SAST: it does not perform inter-procedural data-flow analysis by default. A taint that crosses three function boundaries and two modules may not be detected without explicit taint mode rules. For deep data-flow analysis, CodeQL's semantic approach is more powerful — Semgrep is faster and more accessible.

Semgrep rules look like the code they find. You write a pattern that resembles a dangerous code snippet, and Semgrep finds every place in your codebase that matches it — quickly, across many languages, without needing a PhD in program analysis.

cards.title: DAST: Black-Box Testing a Running Application
cards.teaser: Dynamic Application Security Testing attacks your application from the outside, the way a real attacker would — sending malformed HTTP requests, probing auth endpoints, and observing responses. It finds vulnerabilities that only exist at runtime.

runs.text: DAST tools operate without access to source code. They interact with the application exclusively through its external interfaces — HTTP endpoints, WebSocket connections, form submissions, API responses. This makes DAST the closest automated approximation of a penetration test.
A DAST scan typically proceeds in two phases:

items.text: The tool discovers the application's attack surface by following links, submitting forms, and parsing JavaScript. Modern SPAs require the tool to execute JavaScript (using a headless browser) or be given an OpenAPI/Swagger spec that describes endpoints directly.

The tool replays discovered requests with payloads designed to trigger vulnerabilities: SQL metacharacters, XSS vectors, path traversal sequences, SSRF probes. It analyzes responses for error messages, unexpected behavior, or reflected payloads that indicate successful injection.

runs.text: DAST is uniquely suited to finding:

items.text: — session fixation, weak cookie attributes, JWT misconfiguration.
— SQL injection, command injection, LDAP injection via HTTP parameters.
— endpoints accessible without authentication, IDOR via parameter manipulation.

runs.text: DAST requires a running environment. This places it later in the SDLC than SAST — typically against a staging or pre-production environment. Automating DAST in CI/CD requires care: an active scan can take 30-90 minutes for a medium-complexity application, which is often too long for a PR pipeline. Common patterns: run a baseline (passive) scan on every PR, and schedule a full active scan nightly or pre-release.

Never run DAST active scanning against a production system. Active DAST generates real HTTP traffic with attack payloads — it can corrupt data, trigger alerts, and cause denial of service. Always target a dedicated test environment with a snapshot of production data.

DAST is an automated attacker. It fires HTTP requests at your running app designed to cause misbehavior, then analyzes the responses to determine if something exploitable happened. No source code required — it only sees what a real attacker would see.

cards.title: OWASP ZAP: The Free DAST Standard
cards.teaser: OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) is the industry's default open-source DAST tool — it proxies HTTP traffic, spiders applications, and runs active vulnerability scans. Its CI/CD integration mode makes automated DAST accessible to every team, regardless of budget.

runs.text: ZAP is maintained by the OWASP Foundation and has been the go-to free DAST tool since 2010. In 2023, OWASP transferred ZAP sponsorship to the Software Security Project (SSP), but ZAP remained open source. It supports two primary operating modes relevant to automated testing:

items.text: A passive scan that spiders the target and reports findings visible without active attack. Takes 2-5 minutes. Safe to run on every pull request. Finds missing security headers, information disclosure, cookie attribute issues.

Active scanning mode that fires attack payloads at every discovered endpoint. Takes 30-90+ minutes. Run nightly or pre-release against a staging environment. Finds injection vulnerabilities, broken access control, authentication issues.
Accepts an OpenAPI, GraphQL, or SOAP spec and systematically fuzzes every defined endpoint. Bypasses the crawling phase entirely — ideal for APIs that serve no HTML.

runs.text: ZAP in GitHub Actions CI pipeline (baseline scan):

explanation.code:
- name: OWASP ZAP Baseline Scan
  uses: zaproxy/action-baseline@v0.10.0
  with:
    target: 'https://staging.example.com'
    rules_file_name: '.zap/rules.tsv'
    cmd_options: '-a'
  # Fails the build on WARN or FAIL alerts;
  # individual rules can be set to IGNORE in rules.tsv

runs.text: ZAP produces an HTML report and a machine-readable JSON/XML output suitable for ingestion by CI dashboards. The
rules.tsv
file allows per-rule disposition (FAIL, WARN, IGNORE) — critical for managing false positives without disabling entire scan classes.

ZAP's main limitation compared to Burp Suite is UI/UX for manual testing and the depth of its active scanning engine. For automated pipeline use, ZAP's Docker images and GitHub Actions integration make it the default choice for teams without a commercial DAST budget.

ZAP is a free, open-source tool that sits between your CI pipeline and your staging app, fires attack traffic at it, and tells you what it found. The baseline scan is fast enough for every PR; the full scan goes deep enough for a pre-release gate.

cards.title: Burp Suite: Commercial DAST and Manual Pen-Test Platform
cards.teaser: Burp Suite is the professional standard for web application security testing — a proxy-based platform used by penetration testers and security engineers for both automated scanning and deep manual analysis. Its automation capabilities bridge manual pen-testing and CI/CD.

runs.text: Burp Suite, developed by PortSwigger, comes in three editions. Burp Suite Community is free with limited scanning. Burp Suite Professional adds the full active scanner, Burp Intruder (fuzzer), Collaborator (out-of-band detection), and extensions. Burp Suite Enterprise is the headless, CI/CD-integrated DAST platform designed for automated scanning at scale.
The Burp Suite workflow that distinguishes it from ZAP:

items.text: Burp operates as an intercepting proxy. A security engineer browses the target application through Burp, capturing every request. The scanner then attacks each captured request with full knowledge of the application's real traffic — avoiding the crawling gaps that cause missed endpoints.

An out-of-band interaction server. Payloads are crafted to cause the target to make DNS lookups or HTTP requests to a unique Collaborator domain. This detects blind injection vulnerabilities — SQL injection, SSRF, XXE, Log4Shell — where the vulnerability does not produce visible output in the HTTP response.
The BApp Store contains hundreds of extensions: JWT analyzers, GraphQL scanners, SAML editors, custom active scan payloads. Extensions are written in Java or Python using the Burp Extender API.

The headless enterprise edition exposes a REST API for scheduling scans and retrieving results. Integrates with GitHub, Jira, and Jenkins. Produces SARIF output for upload to GitHub Code Scanning or similar platforms.

runs.text: The distinction between ZAP and Burp Suite in practice:

items.text: is the default choice for automated pipeline DAST with zero licensing cost. Adequate for most OWASP Top 10 coverage in CI.

is the choice for organizations that combine automated DAST with a professional penetration testing program, need blind vulnerability detection via Collaborator, or require deeper active scanning fidelity.

runs.text: Burp Suite is the professional pen-tester's Swiss army knife — it intercepts, records, replays, and attacks HTTP traffic. Its Enterprise edition brings that scanning power into CI/CD. Burp finds vulnerabilities (especially blind ones) that simpler tools miss, at a cost.

cards.title: SCA: Your Dependencies Are Your Attack Surface
cards.teaser: Software Composition Analysis answers a question no other AST technique does: of all the open-source code imported into this project, how much of it has known security vulnerabilities right now? In a typical Node.js or Java project, the answer involves thousands of packages.

runs.text: Modern applications consist largely of imported code. A typical Node.js project with 30 direct dependencies has 800-1500 transitive dependencies — packages that depend on packages that depend on packages. The vast majority of the executable code in the application was written by someone else. SCA exists because SAST cannot analyze that code effectively and DAST cannot attribute a vulnerability to a specific library version.
SCA works by:

items.text: ) to enumerate direct and transitive dependencies with exact versions.

The inventory is checked against NVD (National Vulnerability Database), GitHub Advisory Database, OSV (Open Source Vulnerabilities), and vendor-specific databases. Each match produces a finding: package name, version, CVE ID, CVSS score, and (where known) the patched version.

Some SCA tools (Snyk, Endor Labs) determine whether the vulnerable function in the dependency is actually called by the application. A vulnerability in code you never call cannot be exploited — this analysis dramatically reduces noise.

runs.text: SCA also generates Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — a structured inventory of all components in a software artifact. SBOM formats include SPDX and CycloneDX. Organizations under US executive order EO 14028 on cybersecurity are required to produce SBOMs for software supplied to the federal government.

The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) demonstrated SCA's value at scale. Log4j was a transitive dependency in thousands of applications — many teams did not know they depended on it until SCA tools flagged it within hours of the CVE publication.

SCA is the tool that answers "do any of the libraries I imported have known security bugs?" — across every direct and transitive dependency, matched against public CVE databases. When a new vulnerability drops, SCA tells you in minutes whether you are affected.

cards.title: Snyk, Dependabot, and Renovate: The Auto-PR Pattern
cards.teaser: The auto-PR pattern transforms SCA from a reporting tool into a remediation loop: when a vulnerable dependency is discovered, the tool automatically opens a pull request with the fix. This closes the gap between detection and remediation that leaves organizations exposed for weeks.

runs.text: Three tools dominate the SCA-with-auto-remediation space, each with a distinct design philosophy:

items.text: A commercial SCA platform with deep reachability analysis, proprietary vulnerability intelligence (the Snyk Vuln DB has findings not yet in NVD), and integrations with GitHub, GitLab, Jira, and Slack. Snyk analyzes not just

a dependency has a CVE but whether the vulnerable code path is reachable from the application's entry points. This reduces noise significantly. Snyk also offers Snyk Code (SAST) and Snyk Container (image scanning), positioning itself as a unified developer security platform.

GitHub's built-in SCA and dependency update tool. Two modes: Security Updates (auto-PR when a dependency has a CVE and a patch exists) and Version Updates (auto-PR on every new version, regardless of security). Zero configuration to enable on a GitHub repository — Dependabot reads the package manifest and opens PRs against the default branch. Limitation: no reachability analysis; every CVE in any dependency triggers a PR.

An open-source dependency update bot (Mend.io is the primary sponsor) with significantly more configuration flexibility than Dependabot. Supports grouping related updates into a single PR, scheduled update windows ("only open PRs on Monday morning"), semantic versioning policies (auto-merge patch updates, require review for major), and over 60 package managers. Renovate is the choice for organizations with complex dependency management requirements.

runs.text: The auto-PR pattern only works if the PR gets merged. Common failure modes:

items.text: Dependabot opens 30 PRs in one day after being enabled on a neglected repository. Engineers ignore them. Group updates and schedule windows (Renovate) or reduce the number of tracked dependencies.
Auto-PRs can only be auto-merged if CI passes. Flaky tests permanently stall security updates. Fix flaky tests before enabling auto-merge on security PRs.
A patch version bump that fixes a CVE sometimes changes an API. Integration tests catch this; unit tests do not. DAST or integration test coverage is the backstop for auto-merge safety.

runs.text: Snyk, Dependabot, and Renovate all spot vulnerable dependencies — the difference is what they do next. They open a pull request with the fix automatically, so the patch is waiting for approval rather than waiting for someone to notice the alert.

cards.title: IAST: Instrumented Runtime Analysis
cards.teaser: Interactive Application Security Testing instruments the running application from the inside — embedding a sensor in the process that observes real data flows during testing. The result is security findings with the precision of SAST and the runtime validation of DAST, with near-zero false positives.

runs.text: IAST was introduced by Contrast Security (founded 2014) as a response to the high false positive rates of SAST and the deployment friction of DAST. The central mechanism: instrument the application at the language runtime level — Java bytecode instrumentation, .NET CLR profiling, Node.js module wrapping — so that the sensor sees every data transformation as it happens during test execution.
The IAST sensor is attached to the application process and observes:

items.text: When a value from an HTTP request parameter is stored in a variable, the sensor marks it as tainted. It then tracks that mark through every assignment, concatenation, and method call until the value reaches a sink or is sanitized.

When a tainted value reaches a dangerous operation — a JDBC query, a shell exec, an HTML write — the sensor reports a confirmed vulnerability. Not a pattern match; an actual observation of a dangerous data flow during test execution.
The sensor can observe whether sanitization functions are called and whether they are effective — not just whether they exist in the code path.

runs.text: IAST runs during automated test execution (unit tests, integration tests, functional test suites). The test traffic exercises the application; the sensor reports findings. This means IAST coverage is bounded by test coverage — code paths not exercised during testing produce no findings.
IAST advantages over SAST and DAST:

items.text: — findings represent actual data flows that happened during testing, not static predictions.
— the full call stack from the HTTP entry point to the vulnerable sink is captured.
— IAST runs in the same environment as the application's existing test suite.

runs.text: Commercial IAST tools include Contrast Assess, Seeker (Synopsys), and Hdiv Security. Runtime overhead is typically 5-15% — acceptable during testing, though most teams do not run IAST sensors in production (that role belongs to RASP).

IAST puts a sensor inside the running application during tests. The sensor watches data flow from user inputs to dangerous operations in real time. If a SQL query is built from an HTTP parameter without sanitization — the sensor sees it happen and reports it with a full stack trace. No guessing, no false positives.

cards.title: RASP: Blocking Attacks at Runtime
cards.teaser: Runtime Application Self-Protection embeds a security agent in the application process that intercepts dangerous operations as they execute and blocks them before they can cause harm — turning the application itself into the last line of defense.

runs.text: RASP (the term was coined by Gartner in 2012) operates in production environments. Like IAST, it instruments the application at the runtime level. Unlike IAST, its purpose is not to detect vulnerabilities during testing but to
block exploitation attempts in production traffic.

RASP intercepts at the same instrumentation points as IAST — JDBC queries, shell executions, file operations, deserialization calls — but applies a decision: is the data reaching this operation tainted? If yes, is the operation allowable given the application's expected behavior? If not, terminate the request and alert.

items.text: A RASP agent intercepts every JDBC
call, inspects the query for metacharacters derived from user input, and blocks queries that appear to be injection attempts — even if the application code did not sanitize properly.

RASP can intercept Java deserialization and apply an allowlist of safe classes. This mitigates an entire class of vulnerabilities (like Log4Shell-style gadget chains) regardless of what library is affected.
File system calls with paths that contain
sequences derived from user input are blocked before the OS call is made.

runs.text: RASP vs WAF (Web Application Firewall):

items.text: operates at the network/HTTP layer — it sees HTTP traffic but has no visibility into application internals. A WAF can block a known SQL injection payload pattern in a URL parameter but cannot distinguish a legitimate use from a malicious one based on application context.
operates inside the application process — it sees the fully parsed, decoded, deserialized data as the application sees it. It cannot be bypassed by encoding tricks that fool WAF pattern matching.

runs.text: RASP is a compensating control, not a replacement for fixing vulnerabilities. An organization that relies on RASP to block SQL injection rather than fixing the injection vulnerability has a production incident one configuration change away. RASP buys time; secure code eliminates the risk.

RASP is a bodyguard embedded in the application. It watches every dangerous operation — database queries, file opens, shell calls — and if the input looks like an attack, it steps in and blocks it before any damage is done. It works even if the code has bugs the developers have not fixed yet.

cards.title: False Positives and False Negatives: The AST Reality Check
cards.teaser: Every AST tool makes two types of errors: it reports vulnerabilities that are not real (false positives) and misses vulnerabilities that are real (false negatives). Understanding this tradeoff for each tool type is essential to building a testing program that finds what matters and does not cry wolf.

runs.text: In security testing, the consequences of each error type are asymmetric:

items.text: — the tool reports a vulnerability that does not exist. Cost: developer time wasted investigating and dismissing. Repeated false positives erode trust in the tool, causing engineers to dismiss real findings too. Eventual outcome: alert fatigue.

— the tool misses a real vulnerability. Cost: a potentially exploitable security flaw ships to production undetected. Repeated false negatives erode trust in the program — teams believe they are secure when they are not. Eventual outcome: breach.

runs.text: False positive rates by tool type:

items.text: — high (10–50% in practice). The static model cannot know whether a taint is actually user-controlled or whether a sanitizer in a library it cannot analyze handles it. Pattern-based SAST (Semgrep) has higher FP rates than semantic SAST (CodeQL).

— low (5–15%). DAST confirms a vulnerability by observing the response — if the payload did not trigger the behavior, it was not a vulnerability. But DAST has high false negative rates for code paths not exercised during the scan.

— near-zero false positives (the dependency either has the CVE or it does not), but context-free false positives exist when reachability is not analyzed. A CVE in a test-only dependency or an unreachable function is technically accurate but irrelevant.
— near-zero false positives. Findings represent observed runtime behavior. The false negative risk is untested code paths.

runs.text: Managing false positives in practice:

items.text: Run a new SAST tool in audit mode (no gate, just report) for two weeks. Categorize findings by true/false positive ratio per rule. Disable rules with high FP rates before making them blocking.
When a finding is suppressed (marked as false positive), record why. Review suppressed findings quarterly — application changes can turn a false positive into a true positive.
A finding confirmed by both SAST and DAST has a much higher true-positive probability than one from either tool alone. Prioritize findings that appear in multiple scanners.

runs.text: A false positive is a fire alarm that goes off when there is no fire — annoying, and eventually ignored. A false negative is a fire alarm that does not go off when there is a fire — dangerous. SAST cries wolf a lot. DAST rarely cries wolf but might miss the fire in the back room. A good security testing program layers both.

cards.title: AST in the SDLC: Shift Left Without Abandoning Right
cards.teaser: "Shift left" is the security industry's instruction to test earlier — at code review rather than pre-release. But shift left does not mean shift everything left. Each AST technique belongs at a specific point in the SDLC; the goal is full coverage, not early coverage.

runs.text: Shift left is the principle that security defects cost exponentially more to fix the later in the SDLC they are discovered. An injection vulnerability found by a developer during code review costs an hour to fix. The same vulnerability found in production after a breach costs weeks of incident response, potential regulatory fines, and reputation damage.
The optimal placement of each AST technique in the SDLC:

items.text: Semgrep, Snyk, and SonarLint offer IDE plugins that provide real-time feedback as the developer writes code. This is the leftmost shift possible: feedback before the code is even committed.
Fast SAST (Semgrep) and dependency scanning (Dependabot, Snyk) run on every pull request. Results appear as PR comments or CI failures. Keep this fast: under 3 minutes for SAST, near-instant for SCA.
CodeQL and deeper SAST scans run on every merge to the main branch. Slower (5-20 minutes) but acceptable for post-merge gates. SCA generates SBOM artifacts at build time.
IAST sensors are active during integration and functional test runs. No additional test effort required — the existing test suite generates the traffic that drives IAST coverage.
ZAP baseline scan on every PR deployment to a preview environment. Full active DAST scan nightly and before every release candidate promotion.
RASP blocks active exploits. SCA tools monitor for new CVEs against the production SBOM — a dependency safe at deployment may have a CVE published the next day.

runs.text: The anti-pattern of shift left taken too far: running a 90-minute DAST scan on every pull request commit. This kills developer velocity without improving security — DAST is not the right tool for the PR stage. Tool placement must match tool characteristics.

NIST SP 800-218 (Secure Software Development Framework) formalizes the shift-left principle into a federal software security standard. It requires security testing at each SDLC phase, with the specific controls mapped to development, build, and deployment stages — closely mirroring the layered AST model described here.

Shift left means run the cheapest, fastest security tests earliest. But you still need DAST against a real environment, IAST during integration testing, and RASP in production. Shift left is about putting each tool at its optimal point — not moving all security testing to the IDE.

cards.title: Building a Layered AST Program
cards.teaser: A mature application security testing program is not one tool — it is a deliberate combination of SAST, SCA, IAST, and DAST, each contributing a different layer of coverage, with clear ownership, tuned thresholds, and a defined process for acting on findings.

runs.text: Most organizations start with SCA (lowest effort, highest ROI) and SAST, then layer in DAST, and eventually IAST. The order reflects practicality: SCA requires no application changes; SAST requires rule tuning; DAST requires a staging environment; IAST requires runtime instrumentation. Each layer adds coverage; none replaces the others.
The five characteristics of a mature AST program:

items.text: The security team knows which repositories have which tools active. Coverage gaps — repositories with no AST tooling, or applications with SAST but no DAST — are tracked and addressed.

Critical findings block the pipeline; high findings create tickets; medium and low are reviewed on a cadence. The gate is calibrated: too strict blocks legitimate code; too permissive lets real vulnerabilities through.
Critical: fix within 24 hours. High: fix within 7 days. Medium: fix within 30 days. Low: fix at next convenient release or accept with documented rationale. SLAs without teeth are suggestions.

Security findings are routed to the team that owns the code, not to a central security queue that engineers never read. Findings that are false positives are suppressed with a documented reason and reviewed on a quarterly cycle.

Mean time to remediation (MTTR) per severity. Vulnerability reintroduction rate (same finding reopened within 90 days). False positive rate per tool per rule set. These metrics tell you whether the program is improving the security posture or just generating tickets.

runs.text: The goal of an AST program is not to find every vulnerability — no program can do that. The goal is to make exploitable vulnerabilities progressively harder to ship and progressively faster to remediate. Each tool layer is a filter; the combination of filters narrows the gap between what is possible and what reaches production.

OWASP's Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM) provides a formalized maturity model for security testing programs, mapping practices to maturity levels 1-3. Level 1 corresponds to basic SAST/SCA in CI; Level 3 corresponds to threat-model-driven testing with IAST and automated DAST at scale.

A layered AST program uses each tool where it is most effective, sets clear rules for what blocks shipping and what creates a ticket, tracks remediation times, and measures whether the program is actually making things more secure — not just louder.
